title: An ancient mitochondrial program tunes translation to haem availability.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened all five supplementary data spreadsheets (Supplementary Data 1-5, 62 KB to 1.08 MB) with pandas. Supplementary Data 1 (the haploid gene-trap genetic screen) is 18,753 rows x 7 columns: gene symbol, insertion counts in reporter-low and reporter-high sorted cells, two totals, a Fisher's exact p-value and a Benjamini-Hochberg corrected p-value; 0 duplicate gene rows, 664 rows with no insertions and therefore blank p-values, 220 genes at corrected p<0.05, 1,104 gene entries that are multi-gene composites like 'AATK;MIR657;MIR338;MIR1250'. Supplementary Data 2 = 51 phosphosite rows plus an 1,811-protein iBAQ (intensity-based absolute quantification) sheet over 8 samples. Supplementary Data 3 = 30 peptides x 118 columns. Supplementary Data 4 = 509 protein crosslinks across 8 sheets, nearly all within two proteins. Supplementary Data 5 = ~88 sheets of 3-4 replicate bar-chart values. Also pulled metadata for the mass-spectrometry deposit PXD062916 (open, CC0 licence) and counted the sequencing deposit PRJNA1263803: only 2 raw runs.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The biology (OMA1-DELE1 release on haem scarcity, HRI de-inhibition, conservation to invertebrates, fetal globin induction) comes from the abstract and data availability statement only. Europe PMC's supplementary-file endpoint timed out twice, so the file list came from the full-text XML rather than that service; the files themselves were then fetched directly.

a1_downloadable.note: All five supplementary spreadsheets downloaded with no login; the proteomics deposit PXD062916 is public under a CC0 (public domain) licence. Verified by opening the files.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: In Supplementary Data 1 the screen outcome is already two columns (Pv = Fisher's exact p-value, FCPv = false-discovery-rate corrected p-value) plus the raw insertion counts. Seen in the file.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAIL. The screen table contains no input features at all: the only identifier is a gene symbol string, and 1,104 of the 18,753 entries are multi-gene composites (e.g. 'ABHD14A-ACY1;ABHD14A;ACY1'). Every predictor - sequence, expression, annotation - would have to be fetched from other databases by ~18,753 symbol lookups, with the composite entries needing manual resolution first. Verified by listing the columns.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are documented in the Legend sheet: insertion counts are integers, Pv and FCPv are p-values. Seen in the file.

a5_enough_rows.note: 18,753 gene rows, of which 220 are hits at corrected p<0.05. Counted in the file. Every other table is tiny (51, 30, 509 rows).

a6_fits_laptop.note: Total supplement under 4 MB; raw sequencing (2 SRA runs) and raw mass spectrometry were deliberately not downloaded.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: No specific gene or hit count is quoted in the text I read, so there is nothing to contradict; the table is internally consistent (insertion totals 1,390,120 low and 1,353,600 high match the 'all other mutations' columns).

a8_label_provenance.note: The label is a statistical test on real sequencing counts of gene-trap insertions in sorted cells, not another model's output. The low-vs-high contrast within one library also cancels the usual gene-length insertion bias. Read from the Legend sheet and the counts.

existing_models.name: HemeFinder (bioRxiv 2025 preprint, predictor of haem-binding sites in protein structures)
existing_models.score_and_split: Search snippet reports >94% accuracy at placing haem correctly; split not verified because I only saw the search result, not the paper.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not verified - paper not retrieved in full.

existing_models.name: ESM-2-based autoregressive kinase-substrate phosphosite predictor (bioRxiv 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Search snippet claims state-of-the-art on kinase-specific phosphosite prediction; numbers and split not verified.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Snippet notes existing methods are limited to 7-15 residue peptides, losing structural context.

existing_models.name: HaSAPPy (PLOS Computational Biology, analysis package for haploid gene-trap screens)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not a predictor - it is the counting/statistics pipeline that produces tables like Supplementary Data 1, so it has no held-out score.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model) would be the natural backbone if gene-level sequences were present
backbone.hardware: CPU would suffice for ~19,000 canonical protein sequences, but those sequences are not in the data
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; the supplementary data carries no explicit licence, and the proteomics deposit is CC0

integration.partner_dataset: DepMap (gene dependency across ~1,100 cell lines) or GTEx/Human Protein Atlas expression, joined to supply the missing features
integration.join_key: HGNC gene symbol, which would first need mapping to Ensembl gene IDs and the 1,104 composite symbol strings split
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a cell's requirement for a gene in general (DepMap) predict whether knocking it out switches on the haem-starvation stress response - a question that is interesting but cannot be asked from this file alone, because the file supplies only the outcome and none of the inputs.

controls.positive_control: EIF2AK1 (HRI) itself is in the table as a strong hit (86 low vs 6 high insertions, corrected p = 5.6e-16), along with the haem-pathway genes COX10, COX18 and PARL - a model would have to recover these.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the corrected p-values across genes and confirm any signal collapses; the 664 zero-insertion genes are a natural no-information set.
controls.external_validation: None with the same label: this is a single screen in one haploid cell line with one drug, and no second screen of the same reporter exists that I found.

honest_claim_h3: At best the project could claim 'given public annotation and expression features, we can rank which human genes, when disrupted, switch on a haem-starvation stress reporter in one haploid cell line treated with one drug' - a claim that rests entirely on features the dataset does not contain.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use public gene features to predict which gene knockouts switch on a haem-starvation stress reporter in human cells.
plain_idea.train_on: The one usable table: 18,753 human genes, each with the number of gene-disrupting insertions found in cells sorted for low versus high stress-reporter signal. Features would have to come from elsewhere entirely.
plain_idea.predict: Whether disrupting a gene raises the stress reporter. The truth comes from a single pooled haploid gene-trap screen: cells were sorted by reporter brightness and insertion sites counted by sequencing, then compared with Fisher's exact test.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Labs studying how cells sense haem or iron would get a ranked shortlist of untested genes. Even a failure would show how far gene-level annotation can go in predicting one specific stress-reporter screen.

more_or_better_data.why: The 18,753-row screen measures a different quantity from anything the models I found predict (haem-binding sites, phosphosites), so there is nothing to be bigger than; and the dataset supplies no features to train on.

confidence_score.why: The screen has no replicate arms - it is one low pool and one high pool - so per-gene measurement noise cannot be estimated from the file.

models_beatable.why: No model exists for this task, so there is nothing to beat; the two 2025 predictors I found (HemeFinder, the ESM-2 kinase-substrate model) answer unrelated questions.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition: there is no existing model for this task to run as our baseline, and the features we would add are not a second measurement of the same quantity.

ml_idea: The only candidate task was: predict a gene's enrichment in a haploid gene-trap screen for regulators of a haem-starvation stress reporter (18,753 genes, 220 hits), using features pulled from public resources. The screen label is clean and real, but the file contains nothing except gene symbols and counts, so the whole feature side of the model would have to be built from other databases - and the resulting task (rank genes that control one reporter in one cell line with one drug) has no second dataset to validate against.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: the spreadsheets are under 4 MB and load in seconds, but 16 hours covers resolving 18,753 gene symbols (1,104 of them composite strings) to Ensembl IDs and assembling features from GTEx, DepMap and UniProt - work the paper's files do not do for you.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open Supplementary Data 1 and list its columns: it has seven, and six of them are counts or p-values. There are no input features, which is what kills it (30 seconds).

verdict_reason: Fails Part A3: the one sizeable table (18,753-gene haploid screen) contains only gene symbols and outcome statistics, with zero input features, so every predictor would need ~18,753 cross-database lookups plus cleanup of 1,104 composite symbol strings. The remaining supplementary tables are tiny (51 phosphosites, 30 peptides, 509 crosslinks, replicate bar-chart values) and the deposited sequencing and mass spectrometry are raw. Even granting A3, the task has one cell line, one drug and no second dataset carrying the same label.
